title: Judging the LoCoMo judges
summary: A controlled benchmark of the grading prompts behind published LoCoMo scores. Six grading configurations judged the same 240 answers on the same model snapshot.

benchmark.name: LoCoMo
benchmark.description: A benchmark for long-term conversational memory, whose published scores are often produced with an LLM judge. This measures the graders, not the memory systems.

arms.label: The EverMemOS-derived prompt reconstructed in the community audit
The Mem0 prompt with the dataset's source evidence added
The stricter community variant posted by @dial481

preRegistered.question: How often does each judge accept a known-wrong answer, and does the type of wrong answer matter?
preRegistered.answer: A great deal. Acceptance ranged from 2.5% to 28.8% for specific wrong answers and from 32.5% to 88.8% for vague, on-topic wrong answers. Every judge was substantially more forgiving of vagueness.

preRegistered.question: What does a stricter judge cost in rejected right answers?
preRegistered.answer: Very little when the reference answer is correct. Across 479 scored right answers, there was one rejection. The tradeoff appears when the reference answer itself is wrong.

preRegistered.question: Is "the LoCoMo score" one stable instrument or several?
preRegistered.answer: Several. On identical answers, agreement with the labels ranged from 60.8% to 87.9% depending only on the grader.

preRegistered.question: Does showing the judge the source evidence matter?
preRegistered.answer: Yes. In this setup, evidence made the judge more permissive, not more accurate. The evidence-fed configuration accepted 7.7 percentage points more answers overall, with nearly all of the increase coming from vague wrong answers. Its overall agreement was lower, not higher.

preRegistered.question: When the answer key is wrong, does the judge follow the key or the truth?
preRegistered.answer: It depends on the grader. Against a true answer, broken-key following ranged from 10% to 70%. Every grader accepted all 20 true answers once the key was corrected.

judgePrompts.provenance: already present in the LoCoMo ecosystem or community discussion

abstainPolicy.description: Unparseable responses were recorded as neutral rather than converted into rejections.

result.primary: Changing only the grader moved agreement with the same screened labels from 60.8% to 87.9%. Every grader was much more likely to accept a vague, on-topic wrong answer than a specific wrong answer.
result.interpretation: This is a benchmark of graders, not memory systems. It does not rank or re-score any memory product, and it cannot establish which published system is better.
result.methodStatement: Per-arm agreement with screened labels over the same items, three judge calls per item-arm cell reduced by strict majority, with 95% Wilson intervals.

population.labels: The candidate pool contained 664 items, screened against the question, reference answer, and dataset evidence. The operator hand-reviewed 255 items selected from flagged cases and a preselected sample. The process excluded 137 candidates, including 52 from the initial main-bank selection, and replaced them while preserving the final 80/80/80 class balance and equal category balance. Labels are therefore screened and sampled, not equivalent to independent annotation by two human raters.

parserNeutral.note: Unparseable responses were recorded as neutral rather than converted into rejections, all of them in the evidence-fed configuration. The evidence-fed items consequently left without a valid majority appear as explicit exclusions.

companionChecks.name: Consistency gate
companionChecks.finding: Three of five applicable graders did not treat equivalent set-answer operations consistently.

companionChecks.name: Corrupt answer key
companionChecks.finding: Against a true answer, broken-key following ranged from 10% to 70%. Every grader accepted all 20 true answers once the key was corrected.

limitations: This is a local, self-run venue: the same operator controls task dispatch, execution, and evaluation.
Pre-registration here is a discipline enforced by this tool, not a proof against the run's own owner — nothing prevents the owner from having altered the record before publishing it.

Run pinning on the harness, model, and loadout axes is enforced by an admission gate at dispatch time. The isolation axis is unverifiable: this configured venue admits both unrestricted and OCI-container execution, so its multi-policy inventory cannot establish containment from admission alone.
Cost figures, where present, are self-reported by this venue and were never independently settled.

Distinct solver and evaluator identities prove agent-distinctness only — each evaluator identity is backed by its own workspace-minted signing key, whose verdict signature this product verifies — not that they are independent real-world parties.

Truth uses screened-operator-sampled admission: a pinned model screens every item and the operator hand-checks the flagged set plus a random sample; this proves screen-hand agreement on that sample, not independent two-human truth.
selfRunDisclosure: Distinct evaluator identities are workspace-minted keys; they prove agent-distinctness, not party-independence, on this self-run venue.
